content: Oswaldo Gonçalves Cruz, commonly known as Oswaldo Cruz, was a Brazilian physician, bacteriologist, epidemiologist, and public health officer. He was born on August 5, 1872, in São Luiz de Paraitinga, São Paulo, Brazil, to Bento Gonçalves Cruz, a physician, and Amália Bulhões Cruz. During his childhood, his family relocated to Rio de Janeiro. At the age of 15, he began studying at the Faculty of Medicine in Rio de Janeiro and graduated in 1892 with a thesis on the role of water as a medium for microbial propagation. Inspired by Louis Pasteur's groundbreaking work on the germ theory of disease, Cruz traveled to Paris in 1896 to specialize in bacteriology at the Pasteur Institute, a leading center for scientific research at the time. His studies were financially supported by his father-in-law, a wealthy Portuguese merchant. Upon returning to Brazil, Cruz encountered a severe outbreak of bubonic plague in the seaport of Santos, which posed a significant threat to Rio de Janeiro. He immediately took action to combat the disease. The mayor of Rio de Janeiro authorized the construction of a facility to produce the serum developed at the Pasteur Institute by Alexandre Yersin and his colleagues. The Pasteur Institute recommended Cruz, who was already in Brazil, to lead this effort. Consequently, on May 25, 1900, the Federal Serotherapy Institute was established to produce sera and vaccines against the plague. Cruz was appointed Technical Director, while Baron Pedro Afonso served as Director General. The institute was located on the Manguinhos farm near Guanabara Bay. In 1902, Cruz became the Director General of the institute, expanding its activities beyond serum production to include basic and applied research and the training of scientific personnel. In 1903, Cruz was appointed Director General of Public Health, a role equivalent to today's Minister of Health. Using the Federal Serotherapy Institute as a technical and scientific base, he launched a series of ambitious public health campaigns. His first major challenge was addressing yellow fever epidemics, which had earned Rio de Janeiro the grim nickname Foreigners' Grave. Between 1897 and 1906, 4,000 European immigrants had died from the disease. Cruz implemented measures such as mandatory case reporting, isolation of infected individuals, treatment with sera produced at Manguinhos, and the extermination of rats in the city, successfully curbing the bubonic plague. In 1904, a smallpox epidemic threatened Rio de Janeiro, with over 1,800 hospitalizations in the first five months of the year. Although a law mandating smallpox vaccination for children had existed since 1837, it had never been enforced. On June 9, 1904, Cruz proposed a bill to Congress to reinstate mandatory smallpox vaccination. However, the strict provisions of the law alarmed the public, leading to widespread opposition. Anti-vaccination sentiment grew, fueled by opposition newspapers, labor unions, and even members of parliament. An Anti-Vaccination League was formed, and on November 10, 1904, the Vaccine Revolt erupted in Rio de Janeiro. Violent clashes with police ensued, involving strikes, barricades, and shootings. The government declared a state of siege, and by November 16, the uprising was suppressed, and mandatory vaccination was suspended. However, a severe smallpox epidemic in 1908 led the public to seek vaccination en masse, vindicating Cruz's efforts and earning him widespread recognition. Cruz's international reputation was solidified in 1907 when he received a gold medal at the 14th International Congress on Hygiene and Demography in Berlin for his work in improving sanitation in Rio de Janeiro. In 1909, he retired as Director General of Public Health to focus on the Manguinhos Institute, which was later renamed in his honor. From the institute, he organized scientific expeditions to study health and living conditions in Brazil's interior, contributing to the colonization of various regions. He eradicated urban yellow fever in Pará and led a sanitation campaign in Amazonas, enabling the completion of the Madeira-Mamoré railroad, which had been stalled due to high mortality rates from malaria and yellow fever among workers. In 1913, Cruz was elected to the Brazilian Academy of Arts and Letters. Due to health issues, he resigned as director of the Oswaldo Cruz Institute in 1915 and moved to Petrópolis, a mountain city near Rio de Janeiro. On August 18, 1916, he was elected mayor of Petrópolis and proposed an extensive urbanization plan, which he did not live to see implemented. On February 11, 1917, at the age of 44, Cruz died of kidney failure. Oswaldo Cruz's short but impactful life led to the establishment of a significant scientific and health institution, marking the beginning of experimental medicine in Brazil. His legacy continues to influence Brazilian science, technology, and public health to this day.
